assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock combines the magic-wavelength idea with laser-cooled atoms in a lattice, removing Doppler and recoil shifts while interrogating many atoms at once. It has taken fractional uncertainty to the 1e-18 level and opened relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and a path to redefining the second. As an atomic physicist I see this as a clean, original and broadly consequential advance in precision atomic structure and metrology.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and demonstrated early strontium clocks; Ye's group drove the record accuracy and stability and the many-body clock work. The two-name list is a coherent configuration. Contributions from others (e.g. Lemonde, Pfau and groups in the Sr/Yb community) are not in the supplied credit, so some allocation questions remain.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by many independent groups on several species (Sr, Yb, Hg) with international comparisons, and already used in practice for time-scale work. Timing is ripe; previous prizes covered the frequency comb and ion-trap clocks but not this development.
uncertainties: The exact apportioning of credit beyond the two credited names may be contested.
Whether the clock is judged as a discovery of new physics or as a refinement of metrology, which some may weigh differently.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Bistritzer-MacDonald flat-band prediction and the 2018 observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene created the field of moire materials, a new tunable platform for strongly correlated electron physics. The originality and the rapid spread across condensed matter are striking.
assessment.attribution: Theory credit to Bistritzer and MacDonald is clear, and the decisive experimental breakthrough is Jarillo-Herrero's group. The three-name structure maps well onto theory plus experiment. Related contributions (e.g. Cao and colleagues as lead authors, Dean and others on moire hBN systems) fall outside the supplied credit.
assessment.maturity: Many independent groups reproduced the correlated phases, and the field is mature in its basic phenomenology, though the microscopic origin of the superconductivity is unresolved. Recognition would be timely, with the open mechanism question not preventing the prize for the discovery itself.
uncertainties: The pairing mechanism of superconductivity in the magic-angle system is still debated.
Credit for early experimental and theoretical precursors to twist-angle physics could be disputed.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realised the Hubbard model with controllable parameters, starting with the superfluid-Mott insulator transition and extending to single-site-resolved quantum gas microscopy. It connects atomic physics directly to central problems of many-body physics and quantum simulation, which I consider a distinctive and lasting achievement.
assessment.attribution: The proposal of Jaksch, Zoller and co-workers and later Cirac's contributions, together with Greiner and Bloch's experimental realisations, spread across more than three people. Choosing Bloch, Cirac and Zoller is a defensible but not unique configuration; Greiner's role in the 2002 Mott transition is substantial and would be left out, and the longlist also contains an overlapping Cirac-Zoller entry.
assessment.maturity: Very mature: many groups, widely used quantum-gas microscopes and numerous quantitative benchmarks against theory. Recognition is not premature, although the hoped-for solution of open Hubbard-model questions such as d-wave pairing is only partly delivered.
uncertainties: The attribution is crowded and a fair three-person selection is contested.
Overlap with the separate Cirac-Zoller trapped-ion candidate may complicate how the prize would be scoped.
Whether quantum simulation has solved a problem that classical methods could not remains partial.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED brought strong light-matter coupling into superconducting circuits, enabling dispersive readout and control of qubits and a scalable architecture for quantum processors. The conceptual originality is clear and the impact on quantum technology is large.
assessment.attribution: The 2004 theory proposal (Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin, Schoelkopf) and the first experiment (Wallraff et al.) share credit across five people, so a three-person cut necessarily omits Girvin. Credit within Yale and ETH groups is intertwined, and I am uncertain of the finer details.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed widely and now the basis of leading superconducting-qubit platforms. However, the 2025 prize recognised macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, so a further superconducting-circuit award this soon may be judged premature on timing grounds.
uncertainties: Omission of Steven M. Girvin from a three-person configuration.
Proximity to the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits.
Distinguishing basic discovery from engineering development of qubits.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg blockade provides strong, switchable interactions between neutral atoms, enabling tweezer arrays used for programmable quantum simulation and gate operations. It is a rich atomic-physics idea, building on knowledge of Rydberg states that I find physically elegant.
assessment.attribution: The blockade proposal (Jaksch, Lukin and co-workers), first blockade experiments (Grangier and Saffman groups) and array platforms (Browaeys, Lukin, Bloch, Saffman) share credit among more than four people. The three-name selection is one plausible option among several and leaves out Grangier and others.
assessment.maturity: The area is moving quickly with many groups and rapid scaling, but long-term stability of the interpretation and the eventual role in fault-tolerant computation are not yet settled. Recognition seems somewhat early relative to the established candidates above.
uncertainties: Credit is spread across theorists and experimentalists, and four credited names exceed the three-person limit.
Still evolving platform; achievements may reorder in the coming years.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry uses matter-wave coherence for measurements of gravity, rotation and constants with great sensitivity, and underpins tests of the equivalence principle and gravimeters. It follows naturally from earlier laser-cooling work, and the conceptual leap from light to atoms is meaningful.
assessment.attribution: Bordé's interferometer theory, Pritchard's early atom-optics experiments, and Kasevich and Chu's atomic fountain interferometer are all central. Chu is not in the credited list, and Chu's earlier prize on laser cooling complicates fresh recognition of his role. The three-name selection would be a reasonable but contestable subset.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with practical commercial and field instruments and several independent groups. Impact on fundamental tests is real, yet the headline measurement results beyond existing precision methods are still emerging.
uncertainties: Competing claims between Bordé, Pritchard, Kasevich and Chu make a fair division uncertain.
Whether a decisive discovery as opposed to a technique has been demonstrated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators, followed by observation in HgTe wells and ARPES identification of three-dimensional topological insulators, opened a major area of condensed matter physics. The concept of topology in band structure is original and lasting. It lies outside my own field, so I judge it by general standards.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele's theory, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang's HgTe proposal, Molenkamp's experiment and Hasan's 3D observation are all key; the longlist entry names four people and one of the strongest theory contributors (Bernevig) is absent, and Kane-Mele credit relative to Fu-Kane-Mele and Moore-Balents is a known sticking point.
assessment.maturity: Extensively confirmed by many independent groups, and the interpretation is stable. Recognition is overdue rather than premature, although the Haldane prize in 2016 already covered related topological phases, which might raise questions about marginal novelty.
uncertainties: Disputed credit between theorists and the absence of some key names in the credited list.
Overlap with the 2016 prize on topological phase transitions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cooling and controlling molecules extends laser-cooling physics to complex internal structure, supporting precision tests such as the electron electric dipole moment and ultracold chemistry. It is a natural extension of atomic methods, although it is more of a progressive development than a single transformative discovery.
assessment.attribution: DeMille, Doyle and Ye all made major contributions, though the overlap with the separate direct laser cooling entry means the same people appear in related candidates. Ye already appears in a stronger entry above, which makes a second prize configuration involving him awkward.
assessment.maturity: Recent, still developing, with the most important physics results (e.g. new-physics bounds from eEDM) partly achieved but ongoing. Recognition looks somewhat premature compared with candidates above.
uncertainties: Overlap between this and the direct laser cooling candidate and the shared laureates.
Whether the main impact is realised yet or still prospective.
